source.name: API + TypeScript Conventions
source.description: Backend conventions that the team applies on top of the project-specific rules in team-standards.json. Covers NestJS dependency injection, async/error handling, HTTP API design, TypeScript type safety, and security basics. Each rule is actionable on a small diff — no architecture-scale guidance.

rules.title: Inbound HTTP DTOs must carry class-validator decorators
rules.description: Any class used as the type of a controller method's `@Body()`, `@Query()`, or `@Param()` payload must declare each accepted field with a class-validator decorator (@IsString, @IsInt, @IsEmail, @ValidateNested + @Type for nested arrays, etc.). The global ValidationPipe strips unknown keys and rejects malformed values only when the decorators are present — an undecorated DTO accepts arbitrary input silently.

rules.title: Controllers must delegate; business logic belongs in the service
rules.description: A controller method is HTTP shape and DI; everything else moves to the service. No domain branching (`if (order.status === 'shipped') throw …`), no persistence calls (no direct repository injection), no enrichment (no Date.now, no UUID generation). The controller's job is parse, delegate, return.

rules.title: Inject repositories via @Inject(SYMBOL_TOKEN) and the interface type
rules.description: Consumers of a repository must inject the Symbol token, typed as the repository interface — never the concrete class. This keeps the consumer decoupled from the persistence engine. The module wiring binds `provide: TOKEN, useClass: Sqlite…Repository` (or InMemory…, etc.), and a future swap is one line.

rules.title: Always await Promises or attach a catch handler
rules.description: An async function call whose Promise is neither awaited nor handled silently swallows errors and races other code paths. Either `await` the call, return the Promise to the caller, or attach `.catch(err => logger.error(…))` for fire-and-forget paths.

rules.title: Avoid await inside a for/while loop when the iterations are independent
rules.description: Sequential awaits over an array of independent operations serialises them needlessly. Use `Promise.all(items.map(…))` (or `Promise.allSettled` when failure isolation matters) to parallelise. Only keep the sequential form when each iteration genuinely depends on the previous one's resolved value.

examples.good: const results = await Promise.all(ids.map((id) => this.orders.fetch(id)));

rules.title: Throw the typed @nestjs/common HttpException subclass, not a raw Error
rules.description: Inside a controller or service that bubbles up to HTTP, prefer the typed exceptions Nest ships with — `NotFoundException`, `BadRequestException`, `ConflictException`, `ForbiddenException` — over `throw new Error(…)`. The Nest exception filter renders typed exceptions with the right status code and a structured body; raw Errors collapse to a 500.

rules.title: Avoid the non-null assertion operator (!)
rules.description: `value!` overrides the type system's nullability check; if the value IS null at runtime the program crashes with an opaque TypeError. Prefer a typed guard (`if (!value) throw …`) or a defaulting expression (`value ?? fallback`). Reserve `!` for cases where you've proved (and commented) the runtime invariant.

examples.bad:
const order = this.orders.findById(id)!;
return order.total_cents;

rules.title: Avoid `any`; prefer `unknown` plus a narrowing check
rules.description: `any` disables type checking inside its scope and propagates silently to callers. When the type is genuinely unknown (parsed JSON, external API response), use `unknown` and narrow with a guard before use. Reserve `any` for `// eslint-disable-next-line` with a commented justification.

rules.title: Use the Nest Logger, not console.log
rules.description: `console.log` bypasses Nest's logger and breaks structured log output, log-level filtering, and the test-runner's quiet mode. Construct a Logger with the class name (`private readonly logger = new Logger(MyService.name);`) and use it. Scripts under `scripts/` are the exception — they have no Nest context and can use console.

examples.bad: console.log(`order created id=${id}`);

rules.title: Name magic numbers via a const
rules.description: Hard-coded numeric constants that carry meaning (timeouts, limits, retry counts, port numbers) should be named. The single exception: 0 and 1 in obvious counting contexts. The named const documents intent and centralises the value if it needs to change.

examples.bad: setTimeout(() => this.flushQueue(), 30000);

rules.title: Never read process.env outside ConfigService or main.ts
rules.description: Direct `process.env.X` access in feature code bypasses the typed gateway, defeats fail-fast validation, and creates duplicate parsing logic. Add a typed property + validator on ConfigService and inject ConfigService where you need the value. The only exceptions are `main.ts` (before the DI container is up) and `*.module.ts` files using a `parse*` helper exported from `@/config`.

rules.title: Never log a secret, token, customer email, password, full request body, or full diff
rules.description: API keys, OAuth tokens, webhook signatures, passwords, customer emails, phone numbers, full request bodies, and any other personally identifiable information must not appear in any log statement. They land in CloudWatch, Sentry, and shared log files where access is broader than the running service. Never call console.log or this.logger.log/debug/warn with dto.password, dto.email, dto.customer_email, request.headers.authorization, request.body, or JSON.stringify(dto). Log a stable identifier — request id, user id, customer id, PR node id — or a hash instead. If you must log a key for debug, redact to the last 4 characters.

rules.title: Never interpolate untrusted input into a shell command
rules.description: `child_process.exec` with template interpolation against user input is command injection. Use `child_process.execFile` (or `spawn`) with an args array, OR shell-escape every input. The same rule applies to SQL — use parameterised queries, never string concatenation against user input.

examples.bad: exec(`git checkout ${branch}`, (err, stdout) => { /* ... */ });
examples.good: execFile('git', ['checkout', branch], (err, stdout) => { /* ... */ });

rules.title: Validate untrusted input at the system boundary, not deep inside
rules.description: Trust internal code; validate at the edge. The boundaries are HTTP controllers, queue consumers, file readers, and external-API responses. Internal-only helpers should assume types match — duplicating validation deep in the call graph creates inconsistent rejection and dead defensive code.

rules.title: Pick async/await OR raw Promises in one function, not both
rules.description: Mixing `await someAsync()` with `someOtherAsync().then(…)` in the same function reads as two different control-flow models stitched together. Use async/await throughout when one of the calls needs awaiting; reserve raw Promise chains for fire-and-forget paths or library code.

rules.title: An empty catch block swallows the error silently
rules.description: `catch (err) {}` swallows every failure with no log, no metric, and no propagation. If the error is genuinely safe to ignore (cleanup path, optional feature flag check), at minimum log it at debug level. If the error path is unreachable, omit the try/catch entirely.

rules.title: Public methods should declare an explicit return type
rules.description: An exported method or public class member with inferred return type lets a future implementation change silently widen the public surface (e.g. accidentally returning `any` from a refactor). Explicit return types document intent and trip the typechecker when an implementation diverges. Private helpers can rely on inference.

rules.title: Constructor-injected dependencies and private class fields should be marked readonly
rules.description: Any constructor-injected dependency that's reassigned somewhere in the class is almost always a bug. Marking it `readonly` documents the invariant and lets the typechecker enforce it. The same applies to private class fields holding service instances like `private logger = new Logger(...)`, repositories, services, ConfigService, or any DI'd token — they should all be `private readonly`. Look for `private foo:` or `private foo =` in any `@Injectable` service or `@Controller` constructor or class body — every one of those should be `private readonly` unless the field is genuinely mutable internal state.

rules.title: Represent monetary values in the smallest currency unit (cents), not floats
rules.description: JS floats lose precision (`0.1 + 0.2 === 0.30000000000000004`). For prices, totals, and any persisted amount, use an integer in the smallest currency unit (cents for USD/EUR, satoshi for BTC) and name the field accordingly (`total_cents`, not `total`). Format to decimals only at the presentation boundary.

rules.title: Persist timestamps as epoch milliseconds (integers), not Date strings
rules.description: Date.toISOString() at write time + Date parsing at read time costs CPU, locale ambiguity, and silent timezone drift. Store epoch ms as an integer column (matches Drizzle's `mode: 'timestamp_ms'`). Format to ISO/local time only at the presentation boundary.

rules.title: Use @HttpCode to set the response status for non-200 success paths
rules.description: Nest defaults to 200 OK on every controller method except POST (which defaults to 201). A POST that doesn't create a resource should override to 200; a method that returns nothing should use 204. Make the status explicit so the HTTP semantics match the method.

rules.title: Bound `?limit=` and `?offset=` query parameters on list endpoints
rules.description: Every list/index endpoint must enforce a maximum result size. A `@Get()` handler that returns a collection with NO `?limit=` query parameter at all lets a caller pull the entire table in one request. The same problem applies when `?limit=` IS accepted but passed straight through without an upper bound. Either validate via class-validator (`@Min(1) @Max(100)`) on a DTO, clamp in the controller before passing to the service, or default to a small value (25 is typical) when the param is absent. Pair `?limit=` with `?offset=` so callers can page through.

rules.title: API JSON keys use snake_case; TypeScript locals use camelCase
rules.description: Public JSON keys are snake_case (matches GitHub, Stripe, most public APIs). Internal TypeScript identifiers are camelCase. Map at the controller boundary if needed. Don't expose camelCase keys to API consumers — it's an inconsistency they shouldn't have to remember.

rules.title: Don't mutate DTO fields inside the controller or service
rules.description: The DTO is the inbound contract. Mutating its fields (`dto.currency = dto.currency.toUpperCase()`) couples the storage shape to the wire shape and confuses readers. Build a new domain object instead.

rules.title: Validate state machine transitions before mutating
rules.description: A status field with a fixed transition graph (pending → confirmed → shipped, etc.) needs an explicit guard before each transition. Mutating without the check lets a caller ship a cancelled order or confirm a shipped one. Throw a typed exception when the transition is illegal.

rules.title: Public-facing IDs should be UUIDs or opaque tokens, not sequential integers
rules.description: An incrementing integer ID exposed in a public URL leaks the row count (`GET /orders/42` → you have 42 orders) and enables enumeration attacks (`GET /orders/43`, `/44`, …). Use `crypto.randomUUID()` for the public identifier; keep the integer as an internal-only primary key if you need one.

examples.bad:
@Column({ autoIncrement: true })
id!: number;
examples.good:
@Column({ type: 'text' })
id: string = randomUUID();

rules.title: Don't leak internal error details in HTTP responses
rules.description: A 500 response that echoes the stack trace or raw exception message leaks file paths, library versions, and sometimes secret values to anyone hitting the endpoint. Use the Nest exception filter to map untyped errors to a generic body; log the detail server-side via the Logger.

rules.title: Service method names are verbs in the imperative; controllers mirror them
rules.description: Service methods name an action (`create`, `cancel`, `ship`, `confirm`). Avoid noun-only names (`creation`, `cancellation`) or noun+verb compounds (`processOrderCancel`). The controller uses the same verb where possible so a reader can trace the verb through the layers.

examples.bad: this.orders.orderCancellation(id);
examples.good: this.orders.cancel(id);

rules.title: Don't mark a function async when it never awaits and never returns a Promise from outside
rules.description: An `async` keyword on a function that never awaits adds a microtask hop and wraps every return value in a Promise unnecessarily. Drop `async` when the body is purely synchronous. Keep `async` when the function returns a Promise (even if it doesn't await within itself) to make the return type explicit at the declaration.

rules.title: TODO/FIXME comments must reference a tracked issue
rules.description: A `// TODO: handle the cancellation race` comment has no owner, no priority, and no calendar pressure. Either fix it now, file an issue and reference it (`// TODO(#234): handle the cancellation race`), or delete the comment. The same rule applies to FIXME, XXX, HACK, KLUDGE.

examples.bad: // TODO: handle the cancellation race
examples.good: // TODO(#234): handle the cancellation race
